#9843. How Google Out-Iterated the Entire Model Race

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at computeleap.com

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →

The benchmarks are worth discussing. But they are not the story. The story is what the money says. On Polymarket, Google now holds 80% odds for best AI model at the end of November and 72% for end of 2026 — up 31% this month, the single biggest conviction move on the board. The prediction market is not reacting to any single benchmark. It is reacting to velocity.

Here is what Google shipped in the Gemini 4 family since late September:

Three models. Three distinct roles. Six weeks. And the pricing undercuts every competitor at the frontier tier — VentureBeat noted that Carbon's introductory rate matches Claude Sonnet 5.5 while delivering Opus-class performance, and Hydrogen at $1.50/$7.50 is cheaper still.

For comparison: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 costs $8/$40. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra costs $10/$50. Google is not just competing on intelligence. It is competing on the entire cost-per-task curve.

Carbon is not a minor update over Argon. Google's own benchmarks put it first on 15 of 17 evaluations against Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1. The two exceptions: GPT-6 Astra leads on FrontierSWE 2 (software engineering), and Claude Opus 5.5 leads on OSWorld-2.1 (computer control).

The cybersecurity numbers stand out. Carbon leads on CWE-bench (71.0%), ExploitGym (54.8%), and SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) — all self-reported, all tested without guardrails. Whether those numbers replicate independently matters, but Google is clearly building Carbon's identity around security-forward agentic work.

On the financial side, Carbon matched the best model on Hebbia's end-to-end Financial Agentic evaluation and ranked top of 23 configurations on Balyasny's General Financial Intelligence benchmark. On Artificial Analysis' Coding Agent Index v2.0, Carbon (high reasoning, in Antigravity) ranks second at $7.76 per task — compared to $26.54 for Fable 5.2 at maximum effort.

The pricing math compounds. On Zapier's AutomationBench, Carbon scored 53.88% at $2.12 per task versus Fable 5.2's 51.45% at $4.64. Higher accuracy at less than half the cost.

If Carbon is Google's thinking model, Hydrogen is its execution model. Google describes it as "our daily driver for agentic workflows" — designed not for the hardest problems but for the thousands of routine tool-calling, code-generation, and file-processing tasks that make up an agent's workday.

The safety stats are noteworthy: up to 81% less agentic overreach, 12x fewer misaligned actions in tool-use evaluations, and 96.7% on an internal agent honesty evaluation. Google is clearly responding to the "agents that go rogue" narrative with hard numbers.

The most architecturally interesting signal is not either model alone. It is the Orchestrator.

In Google Antigravity, Carbon can coordinate multi-step tasks while delegating routine work to Hydrogen as a worker agent. Google reports that this pattern achieves near-Carbon task success while using about 24% less quota and finishing about 19% faster. Partners reported 2x to 2.8x faster runs with 12% to 23% lower token usage compared to 3.8 Flash alone.

This is Google shipping multi-model workflows as a first-class product — not a prompt-engineering hack, not an open-source experiment, but a productized pattern where the frontier model and the fast model collaborate within one session. If you have been building your own routing layer between expensive and cheap models, Google just made that a platform feature.

💡 The Orchestrator in practice: Carbon handles architectural decisions and complex reasoning. Hydrogen handles execution — tool calls, code generation, file processing. The result is near-Carbon intelligence at Hydrogen's speed and cost. Google reports a 24% token reduction and 19% faster completion.

The Polymarket data is the sharpest signal because it aggregates thousands of bettors with real capital at risk. Here is the current state:

Read those numbers side by side. The market is telling us something the benchmark tables cannot: Google wins the model race. Anthropic wins the agent race. These are two different competitions.

The 31% move on the year-end model market is the largest single-month conviction shift on Polymarket's AI board. But Anthropic's 96% lock on the November agent market — built on Claude Code, computer use, and the tool-calling ecosystem — is equally striking. OpenAI is a rounding error in both.

We have been tracking prediction market intelligence on the model race throughout 2026. The trend is consistent: the crowd assigns "best model" and "best agent" to different companies, and that split has only widened.

The Hacker News discussion on Gemini 4 reveals the tension that benchmark tables hide. User BoorishBears called Argon "the best writing model that's been released in a while" but worried that Carbon follows "the trend of replacing promising models with benchmark-optimized versions." seizethecheese, who runs a local coding-agent benchmark, called Argon "literally the worst model in our initial ranking" — with Opus 5.5 at the top.

That split is instructive. Google's models polarize practitioners more than any other frontier lab's. The gap between Google's self-reported benchmarks and some developers' lived experience remains wider than for Anthropic or OpenAI. Whether Carbon and Hydrogen close that gap will determine whether the Polymarket odds hold.

Another pattern from the thread: multiple users found that Argon at low and medium thinking modes produced higher-quality results than high mode. If confirmed for Carbon and Hydrogen, this suggests Google's thinking models have a sweet spot below their maximum — a cost optimization that is not obvious from the benchmark tables.

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Velocity as Weakness. Three frontier models in six weeks sounds like dominance. It might also be confusion. Developers who just integrated Argon now face a choice: stick with it, migrate to Carbon (which costs 2x after November 30), or route to Hydrogen for speed. Google's own model picker labels them "Code & analysis," "Most complex work," and "Everyday help" — but where does a medium-complexity coding task go? The surface area of decisions just tripled. Meanwhile, Anthropic shipped one model (Fable 5.2) and owns 96% of the agent market. Sometimes the fastest way to win is not to ship three models — it is to ship one that developers can actually reason about.

Lost in the benchmark comparison is a pricing war that is reshaping the economics of frontier AI:

Google is offering frontier-class intelligence at commodity-class prices. Carbon during its intro period costs the same as Sonnet 5.5 — a model positioned one tier below. Hydrogen is even cheaper. If your workload involves high-volume agentic tasks, the cost differential against Fable 5.2 or Astra is 5-7x.

The catch: Carbon's intro pricing expires November 30. After that, it matches Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 — still competitive, but no longer the obvious bargain.

If you are building AI-powered applications in November 2026, here is the actionable takeaway:

Test Carbon before November 30. The introductory pricing makes it the cheapest frontier model available. If your workload fits its strengths (long-horizon reasoning, cybersecurity, multimodal knowledge work), lock in your evaluation before the price doubles.

Explore the Carbon-Hydrogen Orchestrator pattern. If you have been hand-rolling a routing layer between expensive and cheap models, Google just productized that workflow. The 24% token savings with near-Carbon quality is worth benchmarking against your own routing logic.

Watch the agent market, not the model market. The Polymarket split — Google 80% on models, Anthropic 96% on agents — is the most important signal in the data. If you are building agents that need to call tools, navigate browsers, and maintain long-running workflows, the ecosystem matters more than any individual benchmark. We covered this dynamic in our earlier analysis of prediction markets and the model race.

Do not conflate benchmark leadership with developer adoption. Google leads on paper. The HN thread shows a divided community. Test with your actual workloads, not leaderboard scores. We saw the same pattern when Argon launched — strong numbers, mixed field experience.

💡 The Bottom Line: Google's iteration speed — three Gemini 4 models in six weeks — forced the prediction market's hand. But the market is smarter than the headlines: it split the "best model" crown (Google) from the "best agent" crown (Anthropic). If you are only watching one race, you are watching the wrong one.

#9841. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9839. osFoundry के ज़रिए Codex CLI से GitNest में files import और pull request publish कैसे करवाएँ

यह सब हो जाने के बाद Codex CLI osFoundry के किसी GitNest repository पर दो काम कर पाएगा। वह आपके terminal session की files को एक branch पर लिखता है, और तैयार change set को pull request के रूप में बाहर निकालता है, चाहे GitNest के अंदर हो या GitHub या GitLab पर draft के रूप में। Codex खुद कुछ भी commit या push नहीं करता। हर काम Codex CLI connection पर "Needs your approval" के नीचे एक card बनकर आता है, जिस पर files, branch या exact commit छपा होता है। जब तक repository owner click नहीं करता, कुछ नहीं होता।

Connection हमेशा की तरह बनता है: header में key icon, Connected tab, Other MCP client, और Codex CLI जैसा कोई display name। यही name हर card और हर notification पर दिखता है, इसलिए ऐसा नाम चुनें जिसे owner पहचान ले।

Server 59 tools list करता है। इस walkthrough को इन्हीं सात की ज़रूरत है। तीन propose_ tools ही ऐसे हैं जिन पर read-only का निशान नहीं है, इसलिए "writes" के साथ Codex चारों read tools खुद चला लेता है और हर proposal से पहले रुककर आपसे पूछता है। यानी लगातार दो approvals: पहला आपका terminal में, फिर owner का osFoundry में। अगर owner आप ही हैं, तो पहला approval बस यह check है कि Codex वही माँगने जा रहा है जो आपका मतलब था।

Connection किसी GitNest repository को सिर्फ़ project के ज़रिए देखता है। GitNest में repository खोलें और Project section ढूँढें। Picker सिर्फ़ repository owner को मिलता है। Project चुनें, तो toast में "Repository project updated" आएगा। फिर Connected tab में Codex CLI चुनें और Projects के नीचे उसी project के लिए Add to project पर click करें।

File import के लिए native GitNest repository भी चाहिए, यानी ऐसा repository जिसका Git osFoundry में रहता हो। Tool description साफ़ कहता है: "Repository GitNest must be enabled." जो repository सिर्फ़ GitHub को mirror करता है, वह इसके बजाय change set और provider publication वाला रास्ता लेता है।

propose_gitnest_provider_publication owner के linked Git provider account से push करता है, ठीक उस पल जब owner approve करता है। अगर कोई account linked नहीं है, तो उस approval के पास push करने के लिए कुछ नहीं होता। इसमें से किसी भी चीज़ के लिए Codex को कभी GitHub token की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती।

जिस machine पर यह लिखा गया, उस पर Codex installed नहीं है, इसलिए नीचे का session एक simulated Example है। Tool names और argument names live server के tools/list से लिए गए हैं, उस mcp__osfoundry__ prefix के साथ जो Codex जोड़ता है। Repository, files, IDs और जवाब demo content हैं।

osFoundry में bell पर "Codex CLI proposes GitNest file changes" दिखता है। Connection के panel पर card में "Commit GitNest files in shop-api" लिखा होता है, फिर "Commit to branch: codex/ci-workflow" और commit message। "Review all proposed files (2)" खोलने पर हर file का पूरा text दिखता है, diff summary नहीं। Approve and create commit बना देता है। Decline उसे हटा देता है।

उदाहरण: shop-api का Commit GitNest files card, जिसमें दोनों proposed files खुली हुई हैं

उसी दिन बाद में, जब GitNest में एक change set पहले से composed है:

Codex pull request के लिए न branch तय करता है, न title, न target। Schema सिर्फ़ change set, उसका पढ़ा हुआ version और उसका पढ़ा हुआ composed commit ही लेता है। draft: false या कोई दूसरा target_branch माँगने पर request किसी तक पहुँचने से पहले ही लौटा दी जाती है।

Card का title "Open a draft GitHub or GitLab pull request in shop-api" होता है। उस पर "Change set: … · expected version 3", "Reviewed commit: 73e59f27bc4f…", एक "Review change set before approving" link, और एक line होती है कि approval क्या करता है: वह "uses your linked Git provider account to push this change-set branch and open a draft pull request"। Button है Approve and publish। जो repository GitNest में ही रहता है, उसके लिए propose_gitnest_native_publication इसका sibling card बनाता है, "Publish GitNest pull request", जो "creates a publication branch and opens a pull request in this native repository"।

उदाहरण: Needs your approval के नीचे एक provider pull request card और एक native publication card

Card का link GitNest में change set खोलता है। उसके composed commit के checks सबसे ऊपर, review tabs के ऊपर होते हैं, ताकि फ़ैसला लेने से पहले owner वही देखे जो Codex ने देखा।

File import में सिर्फ़ text जाता है। हर entry एक path और उसका पूरा content है, इसके अलावा कुछ नहीं। न file mode, न delete, न binary, और पूरा commit 20 files और 200 KB के अंदर रहता है। इससे card पर हर byte पढ़ा जा सकता है। GitNest में owner का अपना browser upload इससे कहीं आगे जाता है (2,000 files, हर एक 8 MB, कुल 32 MB), क्योंकि वहाँ एक इंसान अपनी files खुद commit कर रहा होता है।

Publication एक composed change set से होता है, Codex की बताई किसी branch से नहीं। Card उस version और commit को pin कर देता है जिसे Codex ने देखा था। अगर click से पहले change set फिर से compose हो जाए, तो osFoundry का recheck proposal को मना कर देता है, बजाय ऐसी चीज़ publish करने के जिसे किसी ने review नहीं किया। Approval के वक़्त वह मौजूदा permissions, repository के risk tiers और required checks, और target भी check करता है। ये rules लोग GitNest में Risk tiers और Required checks के नीचे तय करते हैं, और Codex इन्हें छू नहीं सकता।

GitHub या GitLab पर सिर्फ़ change set की अपनी branch हिलती है। Pull request draft के रूप में खुलता है, और push approval के वक़्त owner के linked account से होता है। Codex वह token कभी नहीं देखता, और आपकी बाकी branches push का हिस्सा नहीं होतीं।

Merge इस list में नहीं है। इनमें से कोई भी proposal ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा एक खुले pull request तक जाता है। उसे कौन merge करेगा, और merge से जो कुछ भी trigger हो, वह repository के लोगों के हाथ में रहता है।

दोनों publication tools पर tools/list में openWorldHint: true होता है, file import पर नहीं। Pull request conversation के बाहर के लोगों को भी दिखता है। एक ठीक से बना client इसे पहले पूछने की वजह मानता है, जैसा Codex यहाँ करता है।

आगे, import को किसी ऐसी branch पर आज़माएँ जिसे अभी कोई इस्तेमाल नहीं करता। Codex से कहें कि एक ही नई file propose करे, जैसे CONTRIBUTING.md या कोई CI workflow, card पर "Review all proposed files" खोलें और approve कर दें। GitNest page बताता है कि repository की तरफ़ change sets, checks और publication एक साथ कैसे काम करते हैं।

#9837. Privacy-First Personal Search Architecture: Three Latency Budgets for Game Reranking

A game search result has a deadline: the player should see a useful ranking before the next click. A private knowledge manager has the same constraint, even when its documents are patch notes, build guides, and personal play logs. Retrieval quality and latency are coupled; optimizing one in isolation produces a system that feels broken.

Short answer: use a bounded local retrieval pass first, reserve expensive reranking for ambiguous top candidates, and make every deadline visible in telemetry.

Picture the request as a short relay race. The query parser normalizes text, a lexical index finds likely game documents, a local vector index widens the candidate set, and a reranker orders only that small set before generation receives evidence. Each runner gets a handoff time. No stage gets to borrow the whole race clock.

Before this split, every query waits for the same heavyweight model. Exact titles pay for semantic work they do not need, while broad queries create a queue behind one another. After the split, exact-name searches can finish in the first tier and only uncertain rankings spend more compute. The important change is predictability, not a magic model.

Start with a policy budget. For a 180 ms interactive target, one reasonable allocation is 15 ms parsing, 55 ms candidate retrieval, 80 ms reranking, and 30 ms evidence assembly. Those are planning numbers, not performance claims. Measure your own device, corpus, and cache state.

I once watched a dashboard report a healthy p50 while a cold index pushed a few requests past 900 ms. The missing field was queue time. Recording queue, retrieval, and rerank timers separately made the decision obvious: when less than 25 ms remained, a second-stage call could only make the response late. That incident also exposed a subtle feedback loop: a slow request held a worker, the next request waited in the same queue, and the resulting timeout looked like a model-quality problem because its candidate list was empty. We fixed the diagnosis by emitting a span when a request entered the queue, then making the fallback decision from the remaining budget rather than from the original 180 ms target. The ranking did not get smarter. The service got honest about what it could finish.

Keep note text, embeddings, and query traces on the device by default. A remote component, if one is allowed at all, should receive a redacted identifier after a policy check. A trace containing the full query can become an accidental second copy of a private journal, so retention and access controls belong in the retrieval design rather than in a later audit.

Use a narrow, versioned contract between stages. The retriever returns IDs, scores, and a reason code; the reranker returns an ordered list, confidence, and elapsed time. Add a schemaVersion and a maximum candidate count. Those two fields prevent a client update from changing score meaning or turning a bounded lookup into a broad scan.

The margin is a routing signal, not a calibrated probability. Calibrate it against labeled queries from the game catalog and the personal notebook separately; short game names and private prose have different typo patterns. I'm not sure one threshold will survive a multilingual corpus, so keep the threshold in configuration and record its version.

The first tier is lexical and cached. It handles exact names, aliases, and recently opened notes with a strict candidate cap. The second adds local vector similarity for paraphrases and spelling variation. The third reranks the top 20 with a heavier model when the score margin is narrow and enough budget remains. A final fallback returns the best available evidence with an explicit low-confidence state.

Do not collapse those paths into one latency metric. Emit queue_ms, retrieval_ms, rerank_ms, candidate_count, selected_tier, and policy. A timeout is an observable outcome, not an exception to discard. Trace context can be propagated with the W3C Trace Context format, while OpenTelemetry gives a vendor-neutral shape for logs and metrics.

The useful alerts are relationships. Rising p95 with a stable candidate count points toward scheduling or storage contention. Falling recall with stable latency points toward index freshness or tokenization. Log a request hash and document IDs, never the note body. Sampling should be deliberate: keep all budget breaches, but sample routine successful traces.

Replay the set with a warm cache, a cold cache, and a busy device. Inject a full queue and a stale index. Test an empty result too. The correct behavior is a fast, explicit “no matching evidence,” not a confident answer assembled from unrelated context.

The failure mode that surprises teams is candidate starvation: a fast lexical stage returns ten near-duplicates, leaving no room for a relevant paraphrase. Track source diversity and deduplicate before reranking. A slower second tier cannot recover a document that the first tier never admitted.

#9834. A $0 page builder for local shops: one form, two short keys, and a beacon that tells a reader from a link preview

Every local shop I look at has the same hole. Five stars on Google Maps, a price list taped to the counter, and a "website" button on the listing that goes to a Facebook page last updated in 2022. About 17% to 43% of small businesses still have no site, depending on which survey you read, and plenty of the ones that do have a page that cannot answer "how much" and "are you open" without a tap.

I built the smallest thing that answers those two questions, and put the bottom tier at $0. This post is the engineering: what it is made of, what it costs to run, and the two design decisions I am still not sure about.

The business reason first, because it shaped the code

Six services a shop could use as its one bio link, priced over 36 months at each vendor's own annual rate, read in November 2026:

The entry tiers land inside a $430 band and the useful tiers inside a $500 one. Price does not separate these products, so I could not compete on price. The only honest differentiator left was what the page contains — which meant the page had to be cheap enough to give away and good enough to be worth the link.

No sign-up is an architecture choice, not a growth trick: the record is created by the request that needs it, and the key is the whole identity.

The beacon: telling a reader from a link preview

Three details in there are the whole analytics stack:

The burst rule came from data: four seconds, more than one distinct ip_hash on the same path. When a page is pasted into Facebook, Slack or iMessage, the preview renderer fetches it within seconds from several addresses — I measured 49 "visits" landing in three seconds from 2–6 IPs after one post. A human reading a link does not do that. The channel rank query becomes:

Open-now in the wrong time zone. The badge was computed from the shop's typed hours against the server's clock, which is Korean. A café in New York read "Open now" at midnight. The fix stores an IANA zone at publish time (tz=America/New_York) and evaluates the hours in that zone; pages published before the fix keep their old behaviour until edited. tests/open_state.mjs is at 97 passing — the case that breaks naive string comparison is a shop that closes at 2am.

Selling features the free plan already had. The pricing page listed "visit stats", "CSV export" and "inbox" as paid; the free plan returned all three. The fix was not copy, it was a table generated from the feature gate itself, so the page cannot drift from the code again.

Pages and Workers on the free tier, D1 on the free tier, Polar as merchant of record so no card data touches the site. At the current volume — single-digit daily visitors, no paying customers — the marginal cost of a published page rounds to zero. If that stops being true, the paid tiers already answer it: $6.99 removes the footer credit and adds a photo gallery and a notice line; $13.99 adds the owner's domain and a one-time build.

The two questions I cannot answer from the code

Does a $0 tier pay for itself? The free page carries a "Free page · MapToSite" footer line. That is marketing if the people who see it are shop owners and noise if they are not. The beacon cannot tell me that yet, because it counts visits, not who is visiting.

Is an edit key better than an account? Less friction, less to breach, and a random string a barber can lose — and I cannot recover it for him. Accounts exist because they make recovery someone else's job; giving that up is a real cost, not a feature.

The comparison pages name the vendor URL and the date each price was read: the Linktree one, and the same table for Beacons, Wix and Squarespace. The builder itself: maptosite-app.pages.dev/create.

I build MapToSite; the $0 tier in that table is mine.

#9830. The Median AI Coding Bill Grew 16x in Ten Months. Only 16% of It Pays for Code.

Posted on Nov 13 • Edited on Nov 13 • Originally published at faheenahmed160.medium.com • AI-assisted

Three 2026 datasets on what coding agents actually cost per developer, where the money goes, and the point where spending more stops producing more.

For years a developer tool cost about $20 a seat. You bought the seats, forgot about them, and nobody in finance ever asked.

That era ended this year. Coding agents are billed by the token, and the token bill behaves nothing like a seat licence.

Three separate datasets from 2026 now show what that looks like in practice. They agree on the direction. The interesting part is what they say about where the money goes.

Jellyfish looked at Claude Code spend across its customer base for its H1 2026 State of AI in Software Engineering report. Between August 2025 and May 2026 the median user went from about $5 a month to $81, a 16x climb in ten months.

Scale Venture Partners asked 38 startups for their monthly code generation spend, seats and tokens together. The answer, published in May: a median of $577 per engineer per month and an average of $1,040. The author puts that at roughly 50 times what a developer tool used to charge per seat.

Gartner went furthest. In June it predicted that AI coding costs will pass the average developer's salary by 2028. Its peer community data, as reported, has roughly a quarter of technology leaders already paying $200 to $500 per developer per month for tokens, and about 6% paying more than $2,000.

That Gartner headline needs one footnote, and Gartner's own analyst supplied it: the prediction uses a global average salary of about $2,000 a month. It is not a claim about a San Francisco pay packet.

Notice that in the Scale data the average is nearly double the median. That gap is the real story.

Jellyfish's May 2026 distribution shows it clearly. More than half of users still spent under $100 that month. The mean was $248. The 99th percentile was $2,452.

Token use follows the same shape. The median Claude Code user's weekly token count stayed flat through 2026, while the 90th percentile tripled, from about 50 million tokens a week to 170 million.

So most of your team costs about what a nice lunch costs. A handful cost what a contractor costs. A per-seat budget built on the average will be wrong for almost everyone on it.

Here is the number that changes the picture.

In Jellyfish's data, generated code is 0.4% of all tokens. Cache reads, the agent re-reading context it has already seen, are 96%.

Cached tokens are billed at a fraction of the normal rate, so the bill is less lopsided than the token count. But it is still lopsided: cache reads and writes make up about 83% of the bill, against 16% for generated output.

You are not paying the agent to write. You are paying it to read. Every turn of a long session carries the whole conversation, every file it opened, and every tool result back through the model again.

That reframes the cost problem. The expensive thing is not how much code you ask for. It is how much context you drag along while asking.

If the heavy spenders were shipping proportionally more, none of this would matter. Jellyfish checked, using Cursor data from more than 300 companies.

Output does tick up again in the very highest band, and the report works out when that is worth it: heavy spend pays off once a merged PR is worth about $69 or more to you. Value a PR at $15 and the top band's net value drops below zero.

Gartner's analyst said the same thing in fewer words: maximising token use "is not directly related to higher productivity gains."

Budget by distribution, not by seat. Look at your own p50, p90 and p99. Set an alert on the tail rather than a cap on everyone.

Keep sessions short. Since the bill is mostly re-read context, a fresh session for a new task is the cheapest optimisation there is. A four-hour session pays for its first hour over and over.

Invest in context files, not context volume. Jellyfish found that each doubling of a team's investment in context files bought roughly 29% more merged PRs per developer per week. A short, accurate project guide beats letting the agent rediscover the codebase every morning.

Route by difficulty. Renames, boilerplate and test scaffolding do not need the frontier model. This is Gartner's recommendation too: small models for frequent simple work, the expensive one for the hard problems.

Measure cost per merged PR. Tokens per developer tells you who is busy. Cost per merged change tells you who is effective.

Jellyfish sells engineering analytics, Gartner sells advice, and the Scale sample is 38 startups from one investor's network. None of them is a neutral census. The Jellyfish spend figures are also specific to its customers and mostly to Claude Code. But three different methods landing on the same skewed curve is hard to dismiss.

The bill is not growing because agents write more code. Generated code is a rounding error on the invoice.

It is growing because agents read more: longer sessions, bigger contexts, more of them running at once. That is good news, because reading is the part you control.

The cheapest token is the one the agent never had to re-read.

#9829. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9826. My DNS Check Script Said OK for 41 of 41 Hostnames. 22 of Them Don't Exist.

Two weeks ago I posted a bash script for finding dangling DNS records, the kind of old CNAME that let spammers send mail as marthastewart.msn.com. A reader went through it and left a comment I couldn't argue with: if dig comes back with SERVFAIL, the script falls through to the curl branch, the fetch fails, and the host gets printed as OK.

I promised a fix. Before writing it I wanted to see how bad the gap really was, so I ran the old script against my own domains from the box I do these checks on.

It printed OK for 41 of 41 hostnames. 22 of them don't exist.

Here's what went wrong, the three DNS answers a check script has to tell apart, and the fixed script.

I pulled every hostname that ever got a certificate on my domains from crt.sh. 13 domains, crt.sh answered for 11 of them (the other two gave a 502 and an HTML error page, twice), 41 unique names.

Old script, default resolver on that machine:

Same script, same list, but with dig pointed at Google's resolver over HTTPS:

The reason is boring once you see it. The box's resolver answers every name, real or not, with 198.18.0.1 and status: NOERROR:

That's a sandbox thing in my case, but you get the same behaviour from ISP resolvers that "helpfully" turn NXDOMAIN into a search page, hotel and airport wifi, and some corporate DNS. If your check script trusts whatever resolver the machine has, it is checking the resolver, not your domain.

Most scripts, mine included, only look for two states: NOERROR (it exists) and NXDOMAIN (it doesn't). There are really three outcomes, and the third one is two different things.

1. NOERROR or NXDOMAIN. A real answer. You can act on it, as long as the resolver isn't lying (more on that below).

2. Some other status: SERVFAIL, REFUSED. The resolver tried and couldn't give you an answer. To see it, I used dnssec-failed.org, a public test domain with deliberately broken DNSSEC:

Two things in there. dig exits 0 on SERVFAIL, so if dig ...; then tells you nothing. And newer resolvers add an Extended DNS Error line that says why it failed. The codes are in RFC 8914, the Extended DNS Errors spec, and they're worth printing when you're debugging a weird host.

The reader's point was that this state shows up in real life when a domain is still registered but its DNS hosting has lapsed, which is often right before it expires. That's exactly the record you want flagged, and the old script called it fine.

3. No answer at all. Timeout, resolver unreachable, VPN dropped mid-run. There's no status line to grep:

In the old script status ends up as an empty string. Empty isn't NXDOMAIN, so it goes on to curl, and curl uses the system resolver, which might give a totally different answer than dig did. I pointed the old script at a dead resolver and it printed OK for does-not-exist-zq8x7.com.

Five test hosts: the DNSSEC-broken domain, a name that doesn't exist, example.com, a Vercel app name nobody has deployed, and a CNAME (www.github.com).

With a resolver that tells the truth (DIG_OPTS="+https @8.8.8.8"):

On the box's lying resolver, and on a dead one:

Both exit with code 2, so a cron job or CI step fails loudly instead of logging a clean run.

And my own 41 hostnames, on the honest resolver: 22 GONE, 19 OK (all HTTP 200), 0 DNSFAIL, 0 UNKNOWN. Same numbers the old script gave on the honest resolver, which is the point. The old script was right when everything worked and wrong in exactly the cases you run it for.

A note on DIG_OPTS: on a network that intercepts port 53, @1.1.1.1 alone won't help, because the "1.1.1.1" you reach is whatever is doing the intercepting. +https (DNS over HTTPS, in dig 9.18 and later) got around that for me.

The general lesson I'm taking from this: any check script needs a way to say "I don't know". A check that can only say OK or broken will pick OK when it isn't sure.

What does your DNS or uptime check print when the resolver itself is the thing that's broken? I'm curious if anyone already runs a canary lookup like this in CI.

#9824. SkyW4lker Exposed: A Growing Microsoft 365 Phishing Threat to American Enterprises

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

SkyW4lker (SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel) is an active device-code phishing kit targeting Microsoft 365 users in the United States, Europe, and other regions. By abusing Microsoft’s legitimate authentication process, the kit can give attackers access to corporate accounts without stealing passwords or bypassing MFA. This puts business emails, sensitive documents, and other Microsoft 365 resources at risk of unauthorized access.

The ANY.RUN team identified 618 sandbox analyses related to SkyW4lker between June and October 21, 2026, with 46% of submissions coming from the United States. Activity increased from 20 analyses in June to 200 in September, highlighting the growing exposure of organizations relying on Microsoft 365.

JavaScript obfuscation (obfuscator.io), Device-Code phishing, Geolocation detection, IP-address detection, CAPTCHA verification

Email attachments (.pdf, .docx, .xls/xlsx and others), redirection links and lure pages (including Google Maps, Google Images, Miro, Zoom and others)

URL patterns: /session_public.php?action= /endpoints/confirm_visit.php /js/url_helper.js /js/endpoint.js /js/client_geo.js

The United States accounts for 47% of SkyW4lker-related sandbox submissions, more than twice the share of any other country. With the campaign exploiting legitimate Microsoft authentication processes and routine business communications, these findings raise concerns for US enterprises about how effectively existing security controls can identify suspicious activity before it leads to account compromise.

SkyW4lker highlights several security risks that organizations need to account for when protecting business-critical systems and employee identities:

Stop account compromise before it disrupts your business.Detect threats earlier and reduce response costs.

You can examine the full SkyW4lker attack chain in this ANY.RUN Sandbox analysis.

The attacker sends the victim a phishing email with a password-protected attachment. Typical subjects involve commercial offers, contracts, invoices, or confidential documents. The attachment is a PDF, DOCX, or XLSX file, and the password is provided in the email body.

The document contains a link to a CAPTCHA page. Some variants include an additional lure page hosted on a legitimate service such as Miro, Google Sites, or Zoom, which redirects the victim to the next step.

Finally, the victim is directed to a phishing page that instructs them to enter a device code on Microsoft’s legitimate authentication page, potentially granting the attacker access to their Microsoft 365 account.

The phishing page relies on obfuscated JavaScript functions and separate script files. Using ANY.RUN’s In-Browser Data Inspection, analysts can examine the page’s DOM and HTTP activity to understand how these scripts operate.

The scripts keep the page in regular contact with the PHP backend and determine the location of the victim from their IP address. Within the page DOM, the main script loads additional modules, sets click handlers on buttons and builds GET requests to the PHP endpoint /session_public.php with the action parameter (start or poll).

With action=start, the script sends the geolocation and IP address of the victim and receives a session ID. After that, it sends a request with action=poll every few seconds to check whether the victim has authenticated.

The other modules of the phishing page are listed below:

Determines the location of the victim from the response of one of three services: ip-api[.]com, ipapi[.]co or ipwho[.]is. The location can also be obtained through the PHP endpoint php/endpoints/client_geo.php.

Base script with helper wrappers for URL handling, such as building GET parameters and appending slashes.

Tracks the state of the victim. It logs the e-mail address, password, browser, MFA status, country and other auxiliary fields used during authentication and sends them to the PHP backend at php/endpoints/accounts.php.

A single phishing URL can be the starting point for uncovering an entire campaign. In the SkyW4lker investigation, identifying the malicious page was only the beginning. Analysts needed to trace related activity, identify additional infrastructure, and determine how far the campaign extended. Traditionally, connecting these findings requires repeated IOC lookups, manual correlation, and searching through previous investigations.

ANY.RUN’s major new upgrade, Related Threat Context, makes this process significantly faster and easier. By bringing connections to previous sandbox investigations and threat intelligence directly into the Interactive Sandbox, it helps analysts discover related threats, reuse existing findings, and expand investigations with fewer manual steps.

With more than 700,000 security professionals and 16,000 organizations worldwide using ANY.RUN, analysts can draw on a vast pool of real-world investigation data to uncover connections that might otherwise take considerably longer to find.

During our SkyW4lker investigation, the new Related analyses section surfaced previous sandbox sessions sharing the same URL patterns. This gave analysts an immediate starting point for tracing related activity instead of manually searching for connections across individual investigations.

Using the distinctive PHP endpoint /session_public.php, we moved into ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Lookup in a single click, discovered additional phishing activity, and expanded the campaign cluster.

The investigation demonstrates the practical value of Related Threat Context: less time spent searching for connections, faster discovery of related infrastructure, and more evidence available to guide the next investigation step.

The same approach can be applied to other suspicious URLs and indicators, allowing SOC teams to build on previous investigations and uncover related threat infrastructure faster.

Tier 1 analysts spend less time on repetitive IOC research, gaining more evidence to support accurate triage and escalation decisions. Tier 2 analysts receive richer investigation context, helping them focus on cases that genuinely require deeper analysis.

By connecting individual alerts to existing threat intelligence, Related Threat Context helps SOC teams shorten investigation cycles, reduce unnecessary manual work, and make better-informed response decisions.

Give your SOC the context they need for faster triage.Cut repetitive investigations. Increase Tier 1 productivity.

Each phishing page has its own backend, so the administration panel is likely to be hosted on the same domain. Further analysis of the Threat Intelligence Lookup results and data from other sources revealed an administration panel at /admin/index.php.

The CSS styles (command-center.css) suggest the following capabilities of the kit:

Further investigation revealed another important finding: SkyW4lker shares several technical components with Gabagool, a credential phishing kit.

A search in ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence for the unique module paths of SkyW4lker url:”/js/client_geo.js” or url:”/js/url_helper.js” or url:”/js/endpoint.js”) also returns sandbox sessions tagged gabagool. Gabagool was first observed on 23 April 2026, two months before SkyW4lker, and has used the endpoint.js and url_helper.js modules since late April and early May. The two kits share several other features:

client_geo.js, url_helper.js, endpoint.js (since July 2026)

client_geo.js, url_helper.js, endpoint.js (since late April 2026)

/assets/private_captcha/public/widget.js?v=4

/assets/private_captcha/public/widget.js?v=4

zt[A-Za-z0-9]{32}op; it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us from 10 August

zt[A-Za-z0-9]{32}op; it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us from 5 August

5200m[.]com/kvme2/ (16 Oct), torvion[.]life/ofulium/ (5 Oct), ghethim[.]com/hyllen/ (28 Sep – 2 Oct)

5200m[.]com/kvme2/ (15 Oct), torvion[.]life/ofulium/ (6 Oct), ghethim[.]com/hyllen/ (8 Oct)

mostly DigitalOcean; shared IP 172.86.85[.]51 (priorispace[.]biz)

session_public.php (device-code phishing)

accounts.php (login and password harvesting)

Moreover, some sandbox sessions tagged gabagool load the kit from directories named skywalker:

goldcreekconcrete[.]com/example/skywalker/ (sandbox session) and goldcreekconcrete[.]com/skywalker/example/ (sandbox session). On goldcreekconcrete[.]org, which also hosted Gabagool (sandbox session), the directory /skyw4lker/skydirectory/ with the same modules appeared on 29 September (sandbox session).

We therefore assess with high confidence that Gabagool and SkyW4lker are built by the same developer. Gabagool harvests logins and passwords through accounts.php, whereas SkyW4lker abuses the device-code flow through session_public.php, so we regard them as two attack modes of one platform. The identical directories on shared hosts may also point to a common operator; however, the available data does not allow us to distinguish one operator from several customers of the same platform.

The SkyW4lker investigation reveals several technical indicators and attack patterns that security teams can use to identify related phishing activity. For organizations, these findings also highlight opportunities to strengthen identity security and reduce the impact of potential account compromise.

Hunt for SkyW4lker’s technical fingerprints. Look for requests to /session_public.php?action=start and repeated /session_public.php?action=poll calls. Check the JavaScript modules and URL patterns identified in this research to uncover related infrastructure.

Connect phishing activity with suspicious sign-ins. Monitor Microsoft Entra ID logs for unexpected device-code authentication, particularly following suspicious emails or document-sharing requests. Correlating authentication events with phishing indicators can help identify potential account compromise.

Expand investigations beyond individual IOCs. ANY.RUN’s newly introduced Related Threat Context puts connected sandbox analyses at analysts’ fingertips, with a one-click pivot to threat intelligence context for deeper threat hunting. In the SkyW4lker investigation, this helped expand the campaign cluster, while further analysis revealed shared infrastructure and code similarities with Gabagool.

Investigate potential follow-on activity. When account compromise is suspected, review subsequent Microsoft 365 activity to identify affected resources, unauthorized access, and possible attempts to target other users.

Give Tier 1 the evidence to make faster decisions.Keep more cases at Tier 1 with 30% fewer escalations.

SkyW4lker demonstrates why organizations need to look beyond traditional phishing prevention and MFA when evaluating identity security. Three priorities deserve attention:

Close authentication policy gaps. Review where device-code authentication is genuinely required. Restrict or block unnecessary use through Microsoft Entra Conditional Access to reduce opportunities for attackers to abuse legitimate authentication flows.

Strengthen detection across email and identity systems. Ensure the SOC can connect suspicious attachments, phishing infrastructure, and unusual authentication events. Better visibility across these stages helps teams identify potential compromises before attackers expand their access.

Reduce investigation time and escalation costs. Equip Tier 1 analysts with historical threat context and clear escalation criteria. Establish procedures for containing compromised accounts and reviewing unauthorized activity, helping Tier 2 teams focus on incidents requiring deeper investigation.

SkyW4lker continues to evolve, with new endpoints, changing URL patterns, and growing activity across sandbox analyses. Its connection to Gabagool suggests that the same developer is supporting both device-code and credential phishing, giving attackers different ways to compromise business accounts through shared infrastructure.

For organizations, the findings highlight a broader security challenge: attackers are increasingly exploiting legitimate authentication processes and trusted business services, making malicious activity harder to distinguish from normal operations.

As phishing kits evolve, security teams need more than traditional email filtering and MFA. Stronger identity controls, visibility into suspicious authentication activity, and access to connected threat context can help SOCs identify attacks earlier, investigate them faster, and reduce the potential impact on business operations.

ANY.RUN provides cybersecurity solutions that help SOC and MSSP teams detect and investigate threats, make faster decisions, and reduce the time and resources spent on incident response.

The company’s solutions include Interactive Sandbox for analyzing suspicious files, URLs, and phishing attack chains, and ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence with Threat Intelligence Lookup, Threat Intelligence Feeds, and Threat Intelligence Reports. Together, these solutions help security teams uncover related threat activity, track evolving attack infrastructure, and strengthen detection with intelligence from real-world investigations.

Today, ANY.RUN is trusted by more than 16,000 organizations and 700,000 security professionals worldwide. The company is SOC 2 Type II certified, with security controls designed to protect customer data.

T1589.002 Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

The SkyW4lker operator collected recipient e-mail addresses to personalise phishing links using the landing-URL suffix ? or ?? after /it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us.

T1590.005 Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

The SkyW4lker phishing kit recorded the visitor's IP address, ISP, organisation and location to profile victims using client_geo.js and the request /assets/php/endpoints/session_public.php?action=start&ip=…&isp=…&org=…&org_type=.

T1583.001 Acquire Infrastructure: Domains

The SkyW4lker operator registered look-alike domains of real companies to host phishing pages using typo-squatted names under Microsoft-themed subdomain chains, e.g. sdocshares.auth.outlook2026common.copilos26.csr-rooflng[.]com and pdocshared.payments2026.outlooks.common.ecmholdlnggroup[.]com.

T1583.001 Acquire Infrastructure: Domains

The SkyW4lker operator obtained free dynamic-DNS subdomains to host phishing pages using flow505.mooo[.]com, bigbrain.chickenkiller[.]com and off365acess.jumpingcrab[.]com.

T1583.003 Acquire Infrastructure: Virtual Private Server

The SkyW4lker operator rented virtual private servers to run the PHP backend using DigitalOcean hosting (50 of 92 backend IP addresses), e.g. 162.243.64[.]121 and 67.205.154[.]32.

T1608.005 Stage Capabilities: Link Target

The SkyW4lker operator staged intermediate pages to forward victims to the kit using public cloud buckets and site builders, e.g. pub-177b3aa5a54d4f9087a649de5ec766d5.r2[.]dev/docsonedrive2026.html, carcabaoperadologistca.fr-par-1.linodeobjects[.]com/document_excel.html and bethom-contracting-llc.mintlify[.]site.

T1566.001 Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment

The SkyW4lker operator sent password-protected attachments to deliver the phishing link using PDF, XLS, DOCX and EML lures named -protected.pdf or DOC <10 random characters>.pdf, e.g. SHA256 9aa0b87974b9b4cd42603833b7ad44257578467d279b315a071108a5ed02c268.

The SkyW4lker operator sent links hosted on legitimate services to pass e-mail reputation checks using Google Sites, Axure Cloud and Smartsheet pages and the maps.google[.]ie/url?q= redirect, e.g. sites.google[.]com/heatherrasekhomes.com/talbert-manufacturing-inc-0049/home.

The SkyW4lker phishing kit relied on the victim opening the landing link to start a phishing session using the path //it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us.

The SkyW4lker operator imitated routine business correspondence to make the lures credible using subjects such as New Submission From , Approved Statement and Fedwire Funds Service Processed-()-.

The SkyW4lker phishing kit placed a CAPTCHA in front of the phishing page to hide it from automated scanners using Cloudflare Turnstile and the self-hosted /assets/private_captcha/public/widget.js?v=4 with /assets/php/endpoints/private_captcha_challenge.php.

The SkyW4lker phishing kit obfuscated its JavaScript to hinder analysis using obfuscator.io-style code (520 of 618 analyses carry the obfuscated-js tag).

The SkyW4lker phishing kit abused the Microsoft OAuth 2.0 device-code flow to obtain the victim's access tokens using login.microsoft[.]com/device and login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/deviceauth while polling /assets/php/endpoints/session_public.php?action=poll&session_id=.

T1056.003 Input Capture: Web Portal Capture

The SkyW4lker phishing kit logged the victim's e-mail, password, browser, MFA status and country to collect credentials using endpoint.js and the backend php/endpoints/accounts.php.

All indicators were observed in ANY.RUN analyses between 23 June and 21 October 2026.

#9823. Count Rows, Not Errors: 7 Data Bugs I Reproduced

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at Medium

To find out whether a write path loses data, count rows in the source of truth after a forced failure or a concurrent run; the error rate will not tell you. In seven bugs I reproduced over the past week, every call that lost or duplicated data returned success, and one independent count caught each bug.

This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. Each case ran on the real software (PostgreSQL 16.4, Kafka 4.4.0, Elasticsearch 7.17.29, Redis 8.10.2, SQLite 3.46.1); only the external payment and webhook providers were simulated. Each section ends with the check that caught the bug.

A migration dual-writes in one Spring @Transactional method: insert into the legacy table, then into the new one inside a try/catch that counts failures and queues the id for repair. I left out the new table's December partition and recorded 20 events, 10 in December.

All 20 calls returned normally, and nothing was logged at WARN or ERROR. The legacy table, the source of truth, held 10 rows: PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction when one statement fails, so COMMIT silently rolled back (pgjdbc 42.7.8 and 42.2.5). None of the 10 queued ids existed in legacy, so repair had nothing to copy.

The savepoint kept all 20 legacy rows, as did autosave=always on the JDBC URL. 2,000 clean writes took 3,150/3,005 ms instead of 2,646/2,850.

Check: after a forced failure, count the legacy table, not the failure counter.

One partition, 40 payouts, read_committed, one transaction per poll of 20. Nothing crashed. One provider call took 12 s, past max.poll.interval.ms (10 s), so a second consumer took the partition and restarted at offset 0. The first, still alive, paid the other 14 payouts of its batch after the handover; its CommitFailedException came about 8 s later.

With a fresh UUID as the idempotency key per attempt, 20 of 40 payouts were paid twice, in both runs and under KIP-848. Kafka looked perfect: committed offset 40, 40 output records. A key derived from the payout, "payout:" + payoutId, turned 60 provider calls into 40 transfers.

Check: count transfers per payout id at the provider.

Two checkouts of one order, 0 to 20 ms apart, each read pending, called the provider, then ran UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending'. The loser's UPDATE matched 0 rows after its charge went out: 100 of 100 orders were charged twice. Claiming before the call brought it to 0:

In production, also pass attempt_id to the provider as its idempotency key; my fake took none.

Check: fire two checkouts 0 to 20 ms apart and count provider calls.

A projector read WHERE global_seq > checkpoint on a BIGSERIAL column. The number is assigned at INSERT; the row becomes visible at COMMIT. If 101 commits before 100, the projector checkpoints 101 and never reads 100. With 8 concurrent writers the checkpoint reached max(global_seq) every run, yet 201 to 214 of 3,228 events were never projected. One writer missed 0.

Storing pg_current_xact_id() per event, reading only tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot()) and checkpointing on (tx_id, global_seq) missed 0 in 8 runs. The price: any open write transaction stalls the projection.

Check: after the drain, events must equal projected rows.

An Elasticsearch reindex fed a BulkProcessor (5,000 actions, 2 concurrent requests), called close(), then swapped the alias. close() is awaitClose(0, NANOSECONDS), so two bulks, 10,000 documents, were still in flight. Counts through the alias right after the swap: 45,676, 68,830 and 70,116 of 100,000 (the 1 s refresh hid the rest). failedItems stayed 0. awaitClose(60, SECONDS) plus a refresh gave 100,000 in 3 of 3 runs.

Check: swap only after awaitClose returns true and the new count equals the source count.

The handler claimed the delivery key in Redis with SET NX PX 30000, then processed. Processing threw, the handler returned 500, and the claim stayed. The retry at t=5 s hit the claim and got a 200 for "in progress"; most providers stop on any 2xx. At t=31 s the claim had expired with no done marker: processed 0 times. Releasing the claim in the catch (random token, Lua compare-and-delete) let the 5 s retry process it once. Answer 409 for in-progress claims.

Check: make the handler throw once, replay 5 s later, count successful runs.

Eight Python processes each added 1 to one row 250 times: read, update, commit. All 2,000 commits succeeded; the counter ended at 250 in six of six runs. Default sqlite3 opens the transaction at the UPDATE, after the read, and the 5 s busy timeout turned contention into waiting, not errors. BEGIN IMMEDIATE before the read gave 2,000. Full write-up here.

Check: N workers add 1 M times each; assert the result is N × M.

Error rates count calls that failed; all seven bugs lived in calls that succeeded. Before I trust a write path:

#9822. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9821. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.
